packet.prompt:
Read only the supplied manuscript images. Do not search for the text, open a
catalogue or edition, or consult an earlier transcription. Do not identify the
work or author. If prior context has already revealed a proposed identification
or reading, stop and report that exposure instead of calling this a blind reading.

Begin with a brief image-only layout survey. Note orientation, columns, running
titles, rubrics, enlarged initials, underlined text, and interlinear or marginal
glosses when visible. Distinguish observations from tentative interpretations
such as main text with commentary. Do not infer author, work, date, or provenance.
A tight crop may not show the layout; say so rather than guessing.

Use those features to choose a few useful spans: headings or question openings,
then connecting prose, transitions or citation chains. Keep quoted lemmata and
commentary separate. Read enough surrounding prose to make a later source match
checkable; a full transcription is not required. State which areas you selected
and which remain unread. Suggest a wider view or an adjacent crop if needed.

Transcribe those spans, preserving physical lines. Label each line with its
image filename and a line number counted from the top of that image. Keep columns
and marginal additions separate. Note overlapping crops rather than treating
repeated lines as additional text.

Retain abbreviation marks when possible. Put proposed expansions in parentheses,
uncertain readings before a question mark, and unreadable text in [illegible].
Describe visible deletions and additions explicitly. Do not supply missing words
from what would make grammatical or philosophical sense. Leave uncertainty visible.

Return the reading as UTF-8 plain text. Include limitations (cropped lines, damage,
uncertain column order) in that same response. This is an unverified image reading.

text:
PACKET-07 - UNVERIFIED IMAGE READING (blind; no outside source consulted, no identification attempted)

Images viewed: image-001 to image-018 (all that exist; image-019 and image-020 are not present).
image-001 = overview of side A; image-002..009 = details of side A.
image-010 = overview of side B; image-011..018 = details of side B.

====================================================================
1. LAYOUT SURVEY (observation)
====================================================================
The object is a book cover / wrapper seen from the inside, built up from several unrelated
pieces of written parchment (and one paper-like strip) pasted together. On each side there are
four distinct components:

SIDE A (image-001)
 (A1) Centre-left: a narrow upright strip, c. 4.5 cm wide and c. 14.5 cm tall, in a very small,
      heavily abbreviated cursive bookhand, dark brown ink. One column only is visible; the strip
      is cut on both vertical edges, so every line lacks its beginning and/or end. About 36 lines.
      Red underlining of some phrases (observation); three red paraph marks. Surface loss at the
      right edge about two thirds down and across the last five lines. No running title or
      enlarged initial visible. Tentative interpretation: the red-underlined words are quoted
      lemmata and the rest is exposition.
 (A2) Right: a larger sheet turned 90 degrees (its lines run vertically up the image), pale brown
      ink, a rounder, earlier-looking minuscule with long ascenders, widely spaced lines, some
      interlinear glosses in a smaller hand. Lower part has line-initial capitals touched with
      orange and green. Looks like verse lines (each line starts with a capital) - tentative.
 (A3) Bottom turn-in, upside down: large formal liturgical script with neumes above the text and
      an orange rubric.
 (A4) Top turn-in: blank except a later mark like "xx".
 Left margin beside A1: a pen trial / mark ("111-" shape) only.

SIDE B (image-010)
 (B1) Centre: a narrow upright strip in the same kind of small abbreviated cursive as A1, c. 4.5
      cm wide; about 34 lines; cut at both vertical edges and overlapped on the right by B3. Red
      underline at two places. Surface loss near the top and at the bottom right.
 (B2) Left: sheet turned 90 degrees in the same pale-brown rounder minuscule as A2. Upper half
      reads like a word list with synonyms joined by a "vel"-type sign (tentative: glossary or
      glosses to verse); lower half has verse-like lines with coloured initials (green/orange).
 (B3) Right: liturgical fragment, upright, large script with neumes, orange initials/rubric
      ("GR", large S, R). Only the line-ends / line-beginnings survive.
 (B4) Top turn-in: a line of neumes only. Bottom turn-in, upside down: liturgical text + neumes,
      orange "II".

Selected for reading: A1 complete as far as legible (the main connected prose); B1 complete as
far as legible; short readings of A2, A3, B2, B3, B4 for orientation. Unread: nothing was left
wholly unlooked-at, but large parts of A1/B1 are only partly resolved (see below).

Conventions: ( ) = my proposed expansion; ? after a word = uncertain reading; [illegible];
[cut] = line cut by the edge of the strip; [damage] = surface loss; _.._ = red-underlined in the
image; ¶ = red paraph. Line numbers are counted from the top of the named image.

Notes on A1: The repeated, fairly secure elements are "fides catholica" (written cath' / kath' with
superscript), "contra quos confitetur", "2us error", "errores", the red-underlined phrases
"ex patre natum", "lumen de lumine", "... genitum non factum etc.", and the last underlined line
beginning "qui propter nos homines". Citation tags "Jo. i." occur three times; "moysi ecce
constitui te deum pharaoni" is read with fair confidence. Numerals ("·v· errores", "2us") are as
seen. Everything marked ?? is little better than a guess at the letter shapes.

Notes on B1: secure or nearly secure strings are "beniuolentie", "2m est valor", "3m ex parte
illius cui", "res viles et modicas", "[d]ecimatis mentam et rutam et omne olus", "res magnas et
preciosas", "[n]arrat val... maxi... li. ... vii.", "capiti reponi iussit", "dare regi vel
principi vestem", "suis dedit pauperi", "imperator", "ad genua sua". The surrounding prose is a
discussion of giving (dare / donatio / pietas) with numbered points; that is an observation of
vocabulary, not an identification.

A1 and B1 are in the same or a closely similar hand and format, but their subject matter differs;
whether they come from one leaf, one book, or two is not determinable from these images.
